Where we left off
\[T_e = \left[\frac{S_0(1-\alpha)}{4\sigma}\right]^{1/4} = 255\ \mathrm{K} \qquad \text{but the surface is } 288\ \mathrm{K}\]

The 255 K is real — satellites measure Earth radiating to space at exactly this temperature
So the question isn’t “why is our formula wrong” — it’s “why is the surface warmer than the planet’s radiation to space?”

Today: close the gap in four steps

Why the atmosphere intervenes (selective absorption)
The simplest greenhouse (one pane of glass — on the board)
The picture professionals use (emission height)
The 125-year-old objection — and how you will break it


Promise the payoff up front: “by 12:40 you can defeat an argument that fooled physicists for 40 years.”

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Two streams of light that barely touch
text:
Two streams of light that barely touch


Sun (5800 K): peaks near 0.5 µm — shortwave
Earth (255–288 K): peaks near 10–15 µm — longwave
Almost no overlap → energy in and energy out are separate bookkeeping


This spectral separation is a gift — it’s why “solar in, infrared out” is a clean split and why the whole subject is tractable. GR5001 callback: they saw the Trenberth-style budget diagram; this is the physics under its two-column layout.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
Who absorbs what


N₂ + O₂ = ~99% of the air — and nearly transparent in the infrared
The absorbers are the vibrating, polar trace molecules: H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, O₃, N₂O
Nearly transparent at 0.5 µm, strongly absorbing at 10–15 µm


One sentence of molecular physics is enough: symmetric diatomic molecules have no dipole moment to grab infrared photons; triatomic benders and stretchers do. Don’t go deeper unless asked.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: The greenhouse effect is a trace-gas effect
text:
The greenhouse effect is a trace-gas effect

“CO₂ is only 0.04% of the atmosphere!”


Correct — and that 0.04% (plus water vapor) is doing all of the work. Remove every trace gas and keep the 99%: Earth freezes.

Reframe the talking point as the actual story. Plant (don’t fully develop) the week-9 distinction: H₂O is the biggest absorber, but it condenses — days of residence, slaved to temperature — so it’s a feedback, an amplifier. CO₂ is the forcing, the control knob. Lacis et al. 2010 ran it: remove CO₂, the water vapor rains out, Earth ices over. Full treatment Nov 5.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
The simplest greenhouse: setup
One atmospheric layer that is:

transparent to shortwave (sunlight passes through)
perfectly absorbing in longwave (nothing gets past it)
radiating \(\sigma T_a^4\) both up and down



BOARD, not slides, for the whole derivation. Two budgets, two unknowns — ask the room to supply each term before writing it. This is the second board derivation of the course (after week 1’s T_e); same culture: they follow, not admire.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
The derivation (record)
Top of atmosphere: what leaves = what enters \[\sigma T_a^4 = \tfrac{S_0}{4}(1-\alpha) \;\Rightarrow\; T_a = T_e = 255\ \mathrm{K}\]
Surface: heated by Sun and by the sky \[\sigma T_s^4 = \tfrac{S_0}{4}(1-\alpha) + \sigma T_a^4 \;\Rightarrow\; T_s = 2^{1/4}\,T_e \approx 303\ \mathrm{K}\]

Pause on what fell out: the ATMOSPHERE sits at the emission temperature; the surface is warmer than both. The layer doesn’t “trap” heat — it re-radiates downward. Kill the blanket metaphor here (blankets suppress convection; Wood’s 1909 rock-salt greenhouse experiment if asked).

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Three surprises from one tiny model
text:
Three surprises from one tiny model

The atmosphere radiates at 255 K — the surface hides beneath it, warmer
The surface receives more energy from the sky than from the Sun (~340 vs ~168 W/m² in the real budget)
It overshoots: 303 K predicted vs 288 K observed


#2 is the intuition-breaker — let it sit. It’s in the observed surface budget (GR5001’s diagram!): downwelling longwave beats absorbed solar at the ground. #3 is the productive failure that drives the next slide.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Why the overshoot? The best kind of wrong
text:
Why the overshoot? The best kind of wrong

The real atmosphere isn’t a perfect absorber (windows, wings)
Deeper: convection short-circuits radiation — ~100 W/m² leaves the surface as evaporation + thermals, not photons
Pure radiative equilibrium would make the lower atmosphere absurdly steep and unstable → convection overturns it and pins the lapse rate ≈ 6.5 K/km


Automating exactly this repair = Manabe & Wetherald 1967 (week 1’s “most influential paper”).

This is the week’s brief vertical-structure aside — the ONLY dose of RCE this week (thread returns Nov 5). GR5001 callback: their week 3 was convection; “you know why air rises — here’s what that does to the greenhouse.” M&W Fig 16 from last week can reappear for one beat.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Where does Earth’s radiation to space really come from?
text:
Where does Earth’s radiation to space really come from?
In the CO₂/H₂O bands the atmosphere is optically thick: surface photons are absorbed and re-emitted many times before escaping.
Effectively, space “sees” radiation not from the ground but from an effective emission height:
\[z_e \approx 5\text{–}6\ \mathrm{km}, \quad \text{where } T \approx 255\ \mathrm{K}\]


Connect back: the 255 K from week 1 is REAL — satellites measure it. This slide says where it lives: ~5.5 km up. The layer model was a cartoon of this.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Add CO₂ → the radiating surface rises
text:
Add CO₂ → the radiating surface rises

More CO₂ → atmosphere more opaque in the IR → z_e rises
Higher = colder (lapse rate!) → planet radiates less to space
Energy imbalance → the whole column warms…
…until the new emission height is back at 255 K
The surface, ~6 km below along the lapse rate, ends up warmer

\[\Delta T_s \approx \Gamma \cdot \Delta z_e \qquad (\sim150\ \mathrm{m\ rise} \approx 1\ \mathrm{K})\]

Walk the 5 steps slowly, twice if needed — this is the mental model to install for the whole course. Note what restores balance: not the surface “trapping” anything, but the planet’s radiating level sliding up a fixed temperature ladder.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
One sentence to keep

Global warming = raising the height from which Earth radiates to space — with the surface dragged warmer along the lapse rate.


Say it, let them write it, move on. This sentence defeats arguments the layer model can’t (next block).

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
This picture makes free predictions

The stratosphere should cool as the surface warms (it sits above the emission level) — observed ✓, and a fingerprint pure solar warming would not produce
No lapse rate → no warming from raising \(z_e\) → the lapse rate itself matters (week 9: lapse-rate feedback)


Stratospheric cooling: predicted by M&W 1967 (they saw it in Fig 16 last week), confirmed decades later by satellites/radiosondes. This is the honest counterweight to “models are tuned” — fingerprint predictions made before the observations existed.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
1900: Ångström vs Arrhenius

“The CO₂ absorption band is already saturated — the center of the 15 µm band absorbs everything within meters. Adding more CO₂ can’t do anything.” — Knut Ångström’s lab assistant, 1900 (paraphrased)

This argument killed interest in Arrhenius’s work for decades. It still circulates today.
By the end of this hour, you’ll be able to break it. (That’s literally the next activity.)

Frame it with respect — it’s a GOOD objection, and the physics community bought it for ~40 years. Don’t reveal the answer yet.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
Look at the actual spectrum


Band center: opaque at 280 ppm, opaque at 560 ppm — Ångström was right about the center
Band wings: visibly deepening — this is where doubling acts


LIVE DEMO if wifi cooperates (U. Chicago MODTRAN): set 280 ppm, note outgoing flux; double to 560; the flux drops ~3 W/m²; zoom the band wings. Students see the forcing in measured-quantity space. Screenshots on this slide are the wifi-failure fallback — rehearse the demo once beforehand.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Why the response is a logarithm (not zero)
text:
Why the response is a logarithm (not zero)
Each doubling widens the effective opaque interval by roughly the same spectral increment:
\[\Delta F \approx 5.35 \cdot \ln\!\left(\frac{C}{C_0}\right)\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} \qquad \approx 3.7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\ per\ doubling}\]

Saturation is why it’s a log — not why it’s zero
This is why climate speaks in doublings, and why ECS is defined per doubling


280→560 ppm and 560→1120 ppm have the SAME forcing. Also note: this one-line formula is how CMIP-model forcings are quoted and compared — the toy is the ruler (bridge beat returns at the end).

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
text:
Your turn: break Ångström (in pairs)
Here is the argument, verbatim:

“The CO₂ band is already saturated — the atmosphere absorbs all the radiation in that band within a few hundred meters. More CO₂ cannot change the energy balance.”

With your partner, write the strongest 3–4 sentence rebuttal you can. Use anything from today. Names on the slip; hand it in.

Circulate with the TAs. Most pairs will find the wings; the deeper rebuttal (emission height rises regardless — a saturated band just means z_e is HIGH, not that it can’t go higher) is what the debrief adds. Slips → participation credit.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Debrief: three independent ways it fails
text:
Debrief: three independent ways it fails

The wings aren’t saturated — and that’s where doubling acts (you saw it in the spectrum)
The emission height rises regardless — saturation means \(z_e\) is high, not that it’s stuck; higher is colder is less radiation
Thin, cold upper layers always radiate less — there is no altitude where “more absorber” stops mattering


Argument 2 is the professional one — flag that pairs who found it were reasoning at the research level. Historical coda, 1 sentence: the 1940s–50s spectroscopy (partly military-funded, Plass et al.) resolved the band structure and revived CO₂ science.

title: Energy Balance Modeling 1
section: Scale-up: radiation in a real climate model
text:
Scale-up: radiation in a real climate model

Line-by-line absorption: physically exact, computationally hopeless at runtime
Models use band schemes (“correlated-k”), validated against line-by-line codes
Radiation is computed in every column, ~100 levels, every 1–3 model hours


Your layer model and a GCM’s radiation code differ in resolution, not in kind.

The point of the scale-up beat every week: demystify. The radiation module of a CMIP model is the N-layer model with real spectroscopy and clever bookkeeping.

Bridge: the toy is the ruler

Backward: Manabe & Wetherald 1967 = today’s chain done right the first time — real spectra + convection-pinned lapse rate → ECS ≈ 2.3 K, within today’s assessed range
Forward: when CMIP models are compared, their CO₂ forcing is quoted through the same \(5.35\ln(C/C_0)\) — the formula you now own

text: Earth system and climate models are critically important tools for climate science — used to study past climate variability, attribute recent trends and extremes, and project the evolution of the climate system under natural and anthropogenic forcing. title: Lab 0c — Climate of New York City
section: 2. Your first climate model — seasonal cycle fit by eye
text:
2. Your first climate model — seasonal cycle fit by eye
Most of the wiggle is the seasonal cycle. Let’s model temperature as:
\[T(d) \,=\, T_0 \,+\, A\,\cos\!\big(2\pi\,(d - d_{peak})/365 days\big)\]
where \(d\) = day of year. Three parameters — and each one means something physical:

\(T_0\) = ______ (what does it mean? what are its units?)
\(A\) = ______ (what does it mean? units?)
\(d_{peak}\) = ______ (the day the cycle peaks — what sets it?)

Your job: pick all three by hand. Run the cell, look at the plot and the error, adjust, repeat. Stop when you think you have a good fit.
When you’re happy: note your \(T_0\), \(A\), \(d_{peak}\) and RMSE — we’ll collect them.

# EDIT THESE THREE NUMBERS, run, look, repeat:
T0    = 10.0    # °C
A     = 5.0     # °C
d_peak = 172    # day of year  (172 = June 21, the summer solstice — is that right?)

doy = df.index.dayofyear
df["t_model"] = T0 + A * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (doy - d_peak) / 365)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.5))
df["t_obs"]["2010":"2011"].plot(ax=ax, lw=0.8, color="k", label="observations")
df["t_model"]["2010":"2011"].plot(ax=ax, lw=2.5, color="tab:red",
                                  label=f"your model: T0={T0}, A={A}, d_peak={d_peak}")
ax.set_ylabel("°C"); ax.legend()

rmse = np.sqrt(((df["t_obs"] - df["t_model"])**2).mean())
ax.set_title(f"your model's error (RMSE): {rmse:.2f} °C")
plt.tight_layout()









Everyone fit the same data with the same model — and got different numbers. That spread is parameter uncertainty, and you just experienced where it comes from. (A computer can minimize the error too, in some mathematically defined manner.)

Few things to notice:

Your three-parameter model explains lot of the variance. What physical fact makes the seasonal cycle so predictable, when next Tuesday’s weather isn’t?
Where did your \(d_{peak}\) end up? The Sun is strongest at the June solstice (day 172) — but that is almost certainly not where you put the peak. Why would the warmest day of the year lag the sunniest one?

text:
2b. The class ensemble
Everyone fit the same data with the same model — so let’s put all of our answers together.
Type the class’s numbers into the cell below (we’ll read them out), then run it.

# --- COLLECTED IN CLASS: replace these with everyone's numbers ---
class_T0    = [10.0, 12.0, 13.5, 11.5, 14.0, 12.5, 13.0, 11.0]   # °C
class_A     = [ 5.0, 10.0, 12.5,  9.0, 13.0, 11.0, 12.0, 14.0]   # °C
class_dpeak = [ 172,  195,  210,  200,  215,  205,  190,  220]   # day of year
# ----------------------------------------------------------------

doy_axis = np.arange(1, 366)

def seasonal(T0, A, d_peak, d=doy_axis):
    return T0 + A * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (d - d_peak) / 365)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))

# every student's model
for T0_i, A_i, dp_i in zip(class_T0, class_A, class_dpeak):
    ax.plot(doy_axis, seasonal(T0_i, A_i, dp_i), lw=1, color="tab:red", alpha=0.35)

# the class average of the parameters
T0_c, A_c, dp_c = np.mean(class_T0), np.mean(class_A), np.mean(class_dpeak)
ax.plot(doy_axis, seasonal(T0_c, A_c, dp_c), lw=3, color="tab:red", label="CLASS MEAN")

# and reality
obs_cycle = df["t_obs"].groupby(df.index.dayofyear).mean()
ax.plot(obs_cycle.index, obs_cycle.values, lw=3, color="k", label="OBSERVED")

ax.set_xlabel("day of year"); ax.set_ylabel("°C"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("every student's seasonal cycle, and the class mean")
plt.tight_layout()

print(f"class spread:  T0 {np.min(class_T0):.1f}–{np.max(class_T0):.1f} °C   "
      f"A {np.min(class_A):.1f}–{np.max(class_A):.1f} °C   "
      f"d_peak {np.min(class_dpeak)}–{np.max(class_dpeak)}")
print(f"class mean :  T0 = {T0_c:.1f} °C,  A = {A_c:.1f} °C,  d_peak = {dp_c:.0f}")

# keep the class-mean model around; we'll compare it in section 3
df["t_class"] = seasonal(T0_c, A_c, dp_c, df.index.dayofyear)

def rmse(col):
    return np.sqrt(((df["t_obs"] - col) ** 2).mean())

indiv = [rmse(seasonal(a, b, c, df.index.dayofyear)) for a, b, c in zip(class_T0, class_A, class_dpeak)]

All three have a seasonal cycle of roughly the right shape and size — the climate model gets the climate broadly right, if a few degrees cold. Even ERA5 is a bit colder than station data (why?).


3b. Now, the weather
Same three series, but zoomed in to individual days.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
for c, col, lab in [("t_obs", "k", "station"), ("t_era5", "tab:blue", "ERA5"), ("t_cmip6", "tab:orange", "CMIP6 model")]:
    df[c]["2010-06":"2010-12"].plot(ax=ax, lw=1.2, color=col, label=lab)
ax.set_ylabel("°C"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("six months of daily temperature")
plt.tight_layout()








ERA5 rides along with the station; the CMIP6 model does its own thing entirely.
To measure that, we compare anomalies — each series with its own seasonal cycle subtracted, so what’s left is mostly the weather. (Without this step the correlation would mostly measure “do they both have summers?”, which mixes information about seasonality and weather.)

# each series minus its own seasonal cycle -> weather anomalies
anom = df.apply(lambda c: c - c.groupby(doyg).transform("mean"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3))
for c, col, lab in [("t_obs", "k", "station"), ("t_era5", "tab:blue", "ERA5"),
                    ("t_cmip6", "tab:orange", "CMIP6 model")]:
    anom[c]["2010-06":"2010-12"].plot(ax=ax, lw=1.2, color=col, label=lab)
ax.axhline(0, color="0.7", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("anomaly [°C]"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("weather anomalies (seasonal cycle removed)")
plt.tight_layout()

print("day-to-day correlation with the station, seasonal cycles removed:")
print(f"  ERA5  : r = {anom['t_obs'].corr(anom['t_era5']):.2f}")
print(f"  CMIP6 : r = {anom['t_obs'].corr(anom['t_cmip6']):.2f}")

  ERA5  : r = 0.95
  CMIP6 : r = -0.01









Discuss (the big ones):

ERA5 tracks the station day-by-day; the CMIP6 model completely ignores it. Why is that not a failure of the CMIP6 model? What should it get right — and did it, in 3a?
All three 20-year means differ (station warmest, CMIP6 coldest). Give two different kinds of reasons why. (One is about what a grid cell is; one is about the model being imperfect.)
Your three-parameter model has a lower RMSE at this station than the CMIP6 model. Is yours the better model? For what, and for what not?

You just compared the observations to one climate model. But there are dozens, built by different groups, with different grids and different choices inside. Here are eight of them at this same location.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8), width_ratios=[2, 1])

# mean seasonal cycle: every model, plus observations
for m in models.columns:
    ax[0].plot(models[m].groupby(models.index.dayofyear).mean(), lw=1, alpha=0.7, label=m)
ax[0].plot(df["t_obs"].groupby(df.index.dayofyear).mean(), lw=3, color="k", label="OBSERVED")
ax[0].set_xlabel("day of year"); ax[0].set_ylabel("°C")
ax[0].set_title("mean seasonal cycle: 8 CMIP6 models vs reality")
ax[0].legend(fontsize=6, ncol=2)

# 20-year mean temperature: where does reality sit?
means = models.mean().sort_values()
ax[1].barh(range(len(means)), means.values, color="tab:orange", alpha=0.6)
ax[1].set_yticks(range(len(means))); ax[1].set_yticklabels(means.index, fontsize=6)
ax[1].axvline(df["t_obs"].mean(), color="k", lw=2, label="station")
ax[1].axvline(df["t_era5"].mean(), color="tab:blue", lw=2, label="ERA5")
ax[1].set_xlabel("20-year mean [°C]"); ax[1].legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()

print(f"model spread: {means.min():.1f} to {means.max():.1f} °C   (multi-model mean {means.mean():.1f} °C)")

station 13.1 °C · ERA5 11.5 °C









Discuss:

Earlier, one model looked ~3 °C too cold and you might have concluded it was simply wrong. Where do the observations sit relative to the whole set of models?
This spread — models disagreeing with each other — is called model uncertainty. What would you report to someone who asks “what is the climate of New York?” using this ensemble?
The warmest model has the coarsest grid, and its nearest cell to Central Park sits over the ocean. Does that make it a bad model, or a model being asked the wrong question?

title: Reference — where our data comes from
text:
⇩ Download this notebook (.ipynb)
Optional reference — we won’t work through this in class.
The CSV files used in Lab 0c didn’t fall from the sky: they were downloaded from three public archives. This notebook shows exactly how, partly so the numbers are reproducible, and partly because getting data is a real skill you’ll need for your final project.
The cells here are not executed when this page is built (the downloads are slow, and the class shouldn’t depend on three servers being up). Download the notebook and run it yourself if you want the data fresh.
All three cover 1995–2014 — the last 20 years of the CMIP6 historical experiment, so they overlap.
import io, json, urllib.request
import pandas as pd

LAT, LON = 40.78, -73.97          # Central Park
Y0, Y1 = "1995-01-01", "2014-12-31"

title: Reference — where our data comes from
text:
1. Station observations — NOAA GHCN-Daily
The Global Historical Climatology Network holds daily records from tens of thousands of stations. Central Park is USW00094728. NOAA’s Access Data Service will hand you a CSV straight from a URL.
Note we ask for TMAX and TMIN and average them: daily mean temperature (TAVG) is missing for many station-years, so (TMAX + TMIN)/2 is the standard workaround. That is a modelling choice, and it is not identical to a true daily mean: checked against ERA5 (which provides both), the midpoint runs about +0.2 °C warm here. ERA5 and CMIP6 below give true 24-hour means, so the three series are not quite like-for-like.

url = ("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/services/data/v1?dataset=daily-summaries"
       f"&stations=USW00094728&startDate={Y0}&endDate={Y1}&dataTypes=TMAX,TMIN"
       "&units=metric&format=csv")

obs = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=180).read().decode()))
obs["DATE"] = pd.to_datetime(obs["DATE"])
obs["t_obs"] = (obs["TMAX"] + obs["TMIN"]) / 2
obs = obs.set_index("DATE")[["t_obs"]]
obs.head()

title: Reference — where our data comes from
text:
2. Reanalysis — ERA5
ERA5 is a weather model run over the whole satellite/observation record, continuously nudged toward observations. The full archive is enormous; Open-Meteo offers a friendly API that extracts a single point for you.
Watch the fine print: you asked for Central Park, but you get the nearest grid point — around 40.81 °N, 74.02 °W, and it represents an average over roughly 30 km, not a park.

url = (f"https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/era5?latitude={LAT}&longitude={LON}"
       f"&start_date={Y0}&end_date={Y1}&daily=temperature_2m_mean"
       "&timezone=America%2FNew_York")

j = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=300))
era = pd.DataFrame({"DATE": pd.to_datetime(j["daily"]["time"]),
                    "t_era5": j["daily"]["temperature_2m_mean"]}).set_index("DATE")

print("grid point actually returned:", j["latitude"], j["longitude"])
era.head()


obs.join(era, how="outer").to_csv("centralpark_obs_era5_1995-2014.csv")

title: Reference — where our data comes from
section: 3. A climate model — CMIP6 from the cloud
text:
3. A climate model — CMIP6 from the cloud
This is the one we’ll use properly later in the course. Every CMIP6 simulation is catalogued in one big CSV; you filter it to the run you want, then open the data straight from cloud storage — without downloading the whole thing (xarray fetches only the chunks you touch).
The search terms are the CMIP vocabulary you’ll learn later: source_id (which model), experiment_id (which experiment), member_id (which ensemble member), table_id (which output frequency), variable_id (which variable — tas is near-surface air temperature).

import xarray as xr

cat = pd.read_csv("https://storage.googleapis.com/cmip6/pangeo-cmip6.csv")
print(len(cat), "simulations in the catalog")

sel_all = cat[(cat.experiment_id == "historical") & (cat.member_id == "r1i1p1f1")
               & (cat.table_id == "day") & (cat.variable_id == "tas")]

sel = cat[(cat.source_id == "MPI-ESM1-2-HR") & (cat.experiment_id == "historical")
          & (cat.member_id == "r1i1p1f1") & (cat.table_id == "day")
          & (cat.variable_id == "tas")]
sel[["source_id", "experiment_id", "member_id", "table_id", "variable_id", "zstore"]]


ds = xr.open_zarr(sel.zstore.iloc[0], consolidated=True, storage_options={"token": "anon"})
ds

Four things bite everyone the first time:

Longitude runs 0–360, not −180–180. Central Park’s −73.97 becomes 286.03 (LON % 360).
Temperature is in kelvin. Subtract 273.15.
The nearest grid cell is ~100 km wide — here it lands at about 40.68 °N, 74.06 °W, partly over water. It is not Central Park.
Model calendars are their own thing (cftime objects, sometimes 360-day years), so converting to ordinary dates takes an extra step.


pt = (ds.tas.sel(lat=LAT, lon=LON % 360, method="nearest")
            .sel(time=slice("1995", "2014")) - 273.15).load()

print(f"grid cell used: {float(pt.lat):.2f} N, {float(pt.lon) - 360:.2f} E")

s = pt.to_series()
s.index = pd.to_datetime(s.index.astype(str))     # cftime -> ordinary dates
s.rename("t_cmip6").to_csv("centralpark_cmip6_MPI-ESM1-2-HR_1995-2014.csv")
s.head()

title: Reference — where our data comes from
section: 4. The same thing, for eight models
text:
4. The same thing, for eight models
One model is one opinion. The lab also uses an ensemble: the identical extraction, looped over eight modelling centres. Each model has its own grid, so “the cell nearest Central Park” is a different patch of the planet in each case — for the coarsest model it lands over the ocean.

MODELS = ["MPI-ESM1-2-HR", "MPI-ESM1-2-LR", "CanESM5", "MIROC6",
          "IPSL-CM6A-LR", "ACCESS-CM2", "NorESM2-LM", "GFDL-ESM4"]

out = {}
for m in MODELS:
    try:
        z = sel_all[sel_all.source_id == m].zstore.iloc[0]
        ds_m = xr.open_zarr(z, consolidated=True, storage_options={"token": "anon"})
        pt_m = (ds_m.tas.sel(lat=LAT, lon=LON % 360, method="nearest")
                       .sel(time=slice("1995", "2014")) - 273.15).load()
        s_m = pt_m.to_series()
        s_m.index = pd.to_datetime(s_m.index.astype(str)).normalize()
        out[m] = s_m[~s_m.index.duplicated()]
        print(f"{m:16s} cell {float(pt_m.lat):6.2f}N {float(pt_m.lon)-360:7.2f}E   mean {s_m.mean():5.2f} C")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"{m:16s} FAILED ({type(exc).__name__})")

models = pd.DataFrame(out)
models.index.name = "time"
models.to_csv("centralpark_cmip6_multimodel_1995-2014.csv")

title: Lab 0d — A bucket: your first time-dependent model
section: 1. From the board: writing down a budget
text:
1. From the board: writing down a budget
A bucket, with water pouring in and draining out. Track the volume of water, \(V = A\,h\):
\[\underbrace{A\,\frac{dh}{dt}}_{\text{accumulation}} \;=\; \underbrace{F}_{\text{in}} \;-\; \underbrace{Q}_{\text{out}}\]

\(h\) = water level [m], \(A\) = bucket area [m²]
\(F\) = inflow [m³/s] — someone pours. The bucket doesn’t decide: this is external forcing
\(Q\) = outflow [m³/s] — the bucket decides, based on its own state and the properties of the hole.

-> The inflow is imposed; the outflow is the system responding to itself — a feedback.
So \(Q\) depends on the system. But how is a question about physics — and different plumbing gives different answers.

title: Lab 0d — A bucket: your first time-dependent model
section: 2. Two drain laws, from first principles
text:
2. Two drain laws, from first principles
Both laws below come from the same move, and it is the move behind almost every equation in this course: decide which two effects dominate, assume they balance, and neglect the rest. Physicists call this a dominant balance. The two cases differ only in which balance we assume.

A hole in the bucket — nothing resists (Torricelli’s law)
Water leaves through a hole of area \(a\) with nothing to rub against, so nothing dissipates its energy. (Careful with case: \(A\) is the bucket’s cross-section, \(a\) is the opening’s — and \(a \ll A\).) Take a parcel of water at the surface, a height \(h\) above the hole, and let it make its way down: the potential energy it gives up shows up as motion, exactly as for a dropped ball.
\[\underbrace{m g h}_{\text{potential energy released}} \;=\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}}_{\text{kinetic energy gained}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{2gh}\]
The balance we just assumed: all of the released potential energy becomes motion — nothing is lost to friction. Inertia dominates; viscosity is neglected.
The volume leaving per second is then the jet’s speed times the area it flows through:
\[Q = a\,v = a\sqrt{2gh} \;\propto\; \sqrt{h}\]
This is Torricelli’s law (1643): the jet leaves at exactly the speed it would have had if it had fallen freely from the surface. It applies to a bathtub plughole, a hole punched in a can, a dam spillway.

Aside — the same result, done more carefully (Bernoulli).
The falling-parcel argument gets the right answer, but the water is not actually in free fall — it is being pushed out by the weight of everything above it. The honest version follows a streamline from the free surface (point 1) to the jet (point 2) and uses Bernoulli’s equation, which says that without dissipation the sum of pressure, kinetic and potential terms is unchanged along the way:
\[P_1 + \tfrac12\rho v_1^2 + \rho g z_1 \;=\; P_2 + \tfrac12\rho v_2^2 + \rho g z_2\]
Three facts collapse it. The surface is open to the air and the jet emerges into the air, so \(P_1 = P_2\) and the pressures cancel. The bucket is far wider than the hole, so the surface descends slowly and \(v_1 \approx 0\). Measuring height from the hole, \(z_1 = h\) and \(z_2 = 0\). What survives is \(\rho g h = \tfrac12 \rho v^{2}\) — the same \(v=\sqrt{2gh}\).
Two things this version makes visible that the falling-ball picture hides: what actually drives the jet (the pressure of the water column, with the atmosphere cancelling from both ends), and the assumption we are leaning on (no viscous dissipation) — which is precisely what stops being true in the next case.



A narrow tube instead — viscosity resists (Poiseuille’s law)
Replace the hole with a long thin pipe — radius \(r\), length \(L\), so the same opening area \(a=\pi r^{2}\) — or with a plug of sand. The picture changes completely.
Fluid touching a solid surface does not slide along it — it sticks. (This is the no-slip condition, an experimental fact about fluids and walls.) So inside the tube the water is stationary at the wall and fastest in the middle: neighbouring layers of fluid are sliding past one another.
Viscosity is the resistance to exactly that sliding. Newton’s law of viscosity says the drag force per unit area between layers is proportional to how rapidly velocity changes across the flow:
\[\tau \;=\; \mu \frac{dv}{dy} \;\sim\; \mu \frac{v}{r}\]
using \(v/r\) because the speed goes from roughly \(v\) at the centre to zero at the wall, across a distance of about the tube radius \(r\). That stress acts over the whole inner wall of the tube, area \(2\pi r L\), so the total resisting force is \(\mu (v/r)\cdot 2\pi r L\).
Meanwhile the water is pushed by the pressure of the column above, \(\rho g h\), acting on the tube’s cross-section \(\pi r^2\).
The balance we now assume is a different one: the pressure force is opposed by viscous drag, and the two are in equilibrium. Nothing accelerates — the flow settles at whatever speed makes push and drag equal, exactly like a falling object reaching terminal velocity. Here viscosity dominates and inertia is neglected, the opposite choice from Torricelli:
\[\underbrace{\rho g h \cdot \pi r^{2}}_{\text{pressure pushing}} \;\sim\; \underbrace{\mu \frac{v}{r}\cdot 2\pi r L}_{\text{wall drag}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v \sim \frac{\rho g h\, r^{2}}{\mu L} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = v\,\pi r^{2} \;\propto\; h\]
The outflow is linear in \(h\). Notice also \(Q \propto r^{4}\): halving the tube radius cuts the flow sixteenfold — which is why water races out of a hole but creeps through soil.

Scaling arguments get the form right, not the constant.
Solving the flow exactly (Poiseuille) gives \(Q = \pi r^{4}\rho g h / (8\mu L)\). Our argument got every dependence right and missed only the factor of 8.
Worth keeping: physics fixes the form of a law; the number in front comes from a full solution or from measurement. Form = the model’s structure; the number = a parameter. Calibrating a model means pinning down the second, not the first.



The real lesson: laws come from assumed balances
Neither derivation solved the full equations of fluid motion. Each one picked two terms, set them equal, and threw the rest away:









assumed balance

Torricelli
potential energy \(\leftrightarrow\) kinetic energy
viscous dissipation


Poiseuille
pressure force \(\leftrightarrow\) viscous drag
inertia (acceleration)



Both effects are always present. Which one you may neglect depends on the situation — for pipe flow the deciding ratio of inertia to viscosity is the Reynolds number. Choose the wrong balance and you get a confident, wrong law.
This is how nearly every equation in this course will be built. Next week we write a balance between absorbed sunlight and emitted infrared, and neglect everything else — and a planet’s temperature falls out of it.


So which law?

Same bucket, different plumbing, different law. Choosing the law is a modelling decision — one to justify from physics, not convenience.
For the rest of today we use the linear law, \(Q = k\,h\), because it is the simplest thing with the right behaviour:
\[A\,\frac{dh}{dt} \;=\; F \;-\; k\,h\]
with \(k\) [m²/s] the drain constant.

title: Lab 0d — A bucket: your first time-dependent model
text:
3. Equilibrium — no time needed

Thought experiment. What if the drain were a pump running at a fixed rate \(c\), regardless of level? Then \(A\,dh/dt = F - c\): a constant. The bucket fills forever, or empties forever, and only sits still if \(F\) happens to equal \(c\) exactly. Equilibrium exists because outflow grows with level.

At equilibrium the level isn’t changing: \(dh/dt = 0\), so inflow = outflow:
\[h^* = F / k\]
Check the units. Then compute it:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

A = 1.0    # m^2
F = 2.0    # m^3/s
k = 1.0    # m^2/s

h_star = F / k
print(f"equilibrium level h* = {h_star} m")

equilibrium level h* = 2.0 m

title: Lab 0d — A bucket: your first time-dependent model
text:
4. Step forward in time
The equation tells us the rate of change right now. So predict a small step ahead, over and over:
\[h_{\text{next}} = h_{\text{now}} + \Delta t \cdot \frac{F - k\,h_{\text{now}}}{A}\]
(This is called Euler’s method — it’s how almost every model marches time forward.)
Fill in the one missing line:

Until you fill it in, the rate of change is zero — so your plot will be a flat line. That flat line is the model telling you it has no physics in it yet.


def run_bucket(h0, F, k, A=1.0, dt=0.1, n_steps=100):
    """March the bucket forward from level h0. Returns times and levels."""
    h = np.zeros(n_steps)
    h[0] = h0
    for i in range(1, n_steps):
        h[i] = h[i-1] + dt * 0.0   # <-- FILL THIS IN: what is dh/dt?
    return np.arange(n_steps) * dt, h

t, h = run_bucket(h0=0.0, F=2.0, k=1.0)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3))
plt.plot(t, h)
plt.axhline(2.0, ls="--", color="gray", label="h* = F/k")
plt.xlabel("time [s]"); plt.ylabel("level h [m]"); plt.legend();








The level rises and settles at the equilibrium — the drain term pulls it there (fuller → drains harder → a stabilizing feedback).

2. A tiny computation — and a preview of Week 2
The emission temperature of a planet is the temperature it must radiate at to balance the sunlight it absorbs:
\[T_e = \left[\frac{S_0(1-\alpha)}{4\sigma}\right]^{1/4}\]
where \(S_0\) is the solar constant, \(\alpha\) the planetary albedo (how reflective the planet is), and \(\sigma\) the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. Next week we’ll derive this and discover why it gives the wrong answer for Earth’s surface — in the most interesting way possible.
For now: run the cell and look at the plot.

S0 = 1361.0      # solar constant [W m-2]
sigma = 5.67e-8  # Stefan-Boltzmann constant [W m-2 K-4]

albedo = np.linspace(0.0, 0.8, 100)
T_e = (S0 * (1 - albedo) / (4 * sigma)) ** 0.25

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot(albedo, T_e, lw=2)
ax.axvline(0.3, ls="--", color="gray")
ax.axhline(255, ls="--", color="gray")
ax.plot(0.3, 255, "o", color="tab:red", ms=8, zorder=5,
        label="Earth: $\\alpha=0.3$, $T_e\\approx255$ K")
ax.axhline(288, ls=":", color="tab:red",

Weather is the state. Climate is the distribution.

Weather: the value right now — a random variable, unpredictable in detail beyond ~2 weeks
Climate: the distribution those values are drawn from — mean, variability, tails — estimated over a chosen period (convention: ~30 years)
Climate change = the distribution shifting, widening, or reshaping — with very different consequences in the tails

“It’s tough to make predictions, especially about the future.”

Scenario uncertainty — you varied \(F\): the pourer decides, not physics (Earth: emissions)

Different ones dominate at different horizons. (Week 11 quantifies this for the real Earth.)
